terms.gloss: with tooth and nail, with might and main
evidence: Traupman 109: tōtō corpore et omnibus ungulīs
terms.comment: Literally “with the whole body and all the claws”: Latin fights with hooves and talons where English has teeth and nails.

terms.gloss: with the teeth; and so holding on for all one is worth
evidence: Cic. Ac. 2.51: rem mordicus tenēre (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: From mordeō. Mordicus tenēre, to hold fast to a thing and not give it up.

terms.gloss: with hands and feet: with all one’s might
evidence: Ter. And. 676: cōnārī manibus pedibus noctēsque et diēs
Ter. And. 161: manibus pedibus obnīxē omnia factūrum
terms.comment: Lewis & Short s.v. manus gives it as manibus pedibusque, “with might and main”; Terence has the two words without -que.

phrases.latin: ut eum ēriperet, manum arripuit mordicus
phrases.english: to snatch it away, she seized my hand with her teeth

phrases.latin: cōnārī manibus pedibus noctēsque et diēs
phrases.english: to strive with hand and foot, night and day

sources: Lewis & Short: ungula · Lewis & Short: mordicus · Lewis & Short: manus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 109.
